subject: physics
title: Mass-spring systems, pendulums and energy in SHM
key_idea: A mass on a spring and a simple pendulum (for small angles) both oscillate with SHM, and their periods depend on only a few quantities. During SHM energy swaps between kinetic and potential, and the total stays constant if there is no damping.

blocks.text: A mass on a spring is pulled down and released. The spring force is proportional to the extension, so the motion is SHM.

items: A larger mass gives a longer period, because it accelerates more slowly.
A stiffer spring (larger k) gives a shorter period.
The period does not depend on the amplitude.
The same period applies for a vertical or horizontal spring, as long as the spring stays in tension (or compression).

blocks.text: This comes from F = −kx and F = ma, which give a = −(k/m)x. Comparing with a = −ω²x gives ω² = k/m, and T = 2π/ω.

items: T = 2π√(m / k) for a mass on a spring.
T increases with mass and decreases with stiffness.
T does not depend on amplitude.

blocks.text: A simple pendulum is a small mass on a light string. For small angles (under about 10°) the motion is close to SHM.

blocks.label: Period of a simple pendulum
where: l = length from the pivot to the centre of the mass (m)

items: A longer pendulum has a longer period.
The period does not depend on the mass.
The period does not depend on the amplitude, for small angles.
T² is proportional to l, so a graph of T² against l is a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π² / g.

blocks.text: Other oscillators can also be SHM, such as liquid in a U-tube. The information you need is given in the question.

items: T = 2π√(l / g) for small angles.
T depends on length and g, not on mass or amplitude.
A T² against l graph has gradient 4π² / g.

blocks.text: As an object oscillates, energy changes between kinetic and potential forms.

items: At the ends of the motion the object is momentarily at rest. All the energy is potential.
At the equilibrium position the speed is greatest. All the energy is kinetic.
In between, energy is shared, and the total is constant when there is no damping.
The kinetic and potential energies each go through two cycles for every one cycle of the displacement.

blocks.label: Total energy
where: A = amplitude (m); this is x₀ in some courses

blocks.text: The total is the maximum kinetic energy, ½m(ωA)², which is ½mv² at the maximum speed. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the total energy.

diagram.alt: Energy against displacement for SHM. Potential energy is a U-shaped curve, kinetic energy is an inverted U, and the total energy is a flat line equal to the peak of each.

x.label: Displacement as a fraction of the amplitude

diagram.alt: A slider showing how kinetic, potential and total energy change with displacement for an oscillator.

outputs.label: Kinetic energy
outputs.formula: 0.5 * m * w * w * max(A * A - x * x, 0)

outputs.label: Potential energy
outputs.formula: 0.5 * m * w * w * min(x, A) * min(x, A)

items: Energy swaps between kinetic and potential; the total is ½mω²A² and constant.
Eₖ is greatest at the centre and zero at the ends; Eₚ is the opposite.
Eₚ ∝ x² and Eₖ ∝ (A² − x²).

blocks.text: Real oscillators lose energy, so their amplitude falls. The topic of damping is covered in full in the next note.

items: Undamped: the total energy stays constant, so Eₖ + Eₚ = constant and the amplitude stays the same.
Damped: resistive forces do work against the motion. Energy is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy.
With damping the total energy decreases with each cycle, so the amplitude decreases over time.
The energy lost in a cycle is the work done against the resistive force.
Without damping, energy is conserved and the amplitude stays constant.
With damping, energy is transferred to the surroundings and the amplitude falls.

checks.q: A 0.25 kg mass hangs on a spring of spring constant 40 N/m. Calculate the period of its oscillations.
Describe the energy changes in one complete oscillation of a pendulum, and state what happens to the total energy if there is no damping.
checks.a: At each end all the energy is gravitational potential energy; at the lowest point all is kinetic energy; energy swaps between the two as it moves. The total energy stays constant.

checks.q: An oscillator has mass 0.40 kg, angular frequency 5.0 rad/s and amplitude 0.12 m. Calculate its total energy and its kinetic energy at a displacement of 0.060 m.

items: Know how Eₖ, Eₚ and total energy vary with both displacement and time.
Against time, Eₖ and Eₚ are both curves of frequency twice that of the oscillation, always positive, and they add to a flat total.
Questions may use other harmonic oscillators, such as liquid in a U-tube. The information you need is given.

blocks.text: Required practical: SHM with a mass-spring system and a pendulum

items.text: Hang different masses from a spring. Displace slightly and time 10 or more oscillations to find T for each mass.
Plot T² against m. The line is straight with gradient 4π² / k.
Vary the length l from pivot to the centre of the bob. Time 10 or more oscillations for each, using a small angle.
Plot T² against l. The gradient is 4π² / g, which gives g.

items: Use a fiducial marker at the centre and time from there.
Timing many oscillations reduces the percentage uncertainty.
Apply conservation of energy to undamped systems: Eₖ + Eₚ stays constant.
For a vertical mass-spring system the potential energy includes both elastic and gravitational parts.
Apply it to damped systems: the total energy falls, and the energy lost equals the work done against the resistive force.
The use of T = 2π√(m/k) and T = 2π√(l/g) is covered with the equations of SHM.
The amplitude is written x₀, so the total energy is E = ½mω²x₀².
Describe the interchange of kinetic and potential energy in words, as well as calculating it.
Sketch and interpret energy–displacement graphs: Eₚ is a parabola with its minimum at x = 0, Eₖ is an inverted parabola, and the total is a horizontal line.
The Eₖ and Eₚ curves cross where x = ±A/√2, where each is half the total energy.
The area under a force–displacement graph is the work done, which links to Eₚ.
